scope: Every timeline and step was read in context and compared with available saved canonical rules/accounts. Selected doubts and recent holdings were checked against primary passages. This is not a fresh complete-opinion review of all authorities or a certification of all current law.
limitations: Most cases were compared against their inherited canonical rule lines, not reread as complete briefs or opinions.
Seventeen fresh primary documents supplied targeted checks, not complete doctrinal negative-treatment research.
Inherited source citations, review status and hashes provide provenance; they do not independently establish accuracy.
Model UCC texts and Restatements require jurisdiction-specific enactment/adoption checks.
The online OLRC preliminary § 1332 page was under maintenance; fresh text comparison used Cornell’s reproduction of the statute.
External Consumers’ Research and FDA later-treatment comparisons do not create new authored case briefs.

basis.comparedRule: A public advertisement is an offer when it is sufficiently definite and leaves no further negotiation necessary to complete the transaction, and the advertiser may not impose new conditions after the offer has been accepted.
basis.inheritedCitation: 251 Minn. 188, 86 N.W.2d 689 (1957). Supreme Court of Minnesota. Murphy, J. Decided December 20, 1957. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that the store's advertisement for a specifically identified fur stole at a stated price, offered to the first customer to arrive, created an offer that Morris Lefkowitz accepted by satisfying those conditions. The store could not then add an eligibility restriction absent from the advertisement. Lefkowitz, the customer and plaintiff below, was the respondent on appeal and represented himself. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc., the merchant and defendant below, appealed an order refusing to alter the trial court's findings or grant a new trial. The Supreme Court affirmed, leaving Lefkowitz's $138.50 damages award in place. 251 Minn. at 189-92, 86 N.W.2d at 690-91. The full opinion concerns two newspaper advertisements published a week apart. On April 6, 1956, the store advertised three new fur coats for one dollar each, available at 9 a.m. the following Saturday on a first-come, first-served basis. The advertisement described the coats as worth up to $100. On April 13, the store advertised two pastel mink three-skin scarfs, described as selling for $89.50, and one black lapin stole, described as worth $139.50, for one dollar each. The second advertisement again specified Saturday at 9 a.m. and first-come, first-served availability. The lapin stole was the item that ultimately supported the damages award.

The North Dakota Supreme Court held that Donald Wucherpfennig failed to accept Elizabeth Dooley's offer to sell her interest in inherited farmland before she revoked it. The response sent through the estate's attorney expressed readiness to proceed and sought further information, but it did not communicate a definite present commitment to buy on the offered terms. The court affirmed dismissal of Donald's claim for specific performance, the remedy that would have required Elizabeth to convey her interest. Donald was the plaintiff and appellant; Elizabeth, his sister, was the defendant and appellee. Their sister Louise Grettum and persons claiming interests in the land were also named defendants, although the disputed sale concerned Elizabeth's share. 351 N.W.2d at 443-45.

before.note: The Code writes Wood in: exclusive dealing implies best efforts, and output or requirements mean quantities produced or needed in good faith.

after.note: For goods, § 2-306(2) imposes best efforts in exclusive dealing unless otherwise agreed; subsection (1) separately measures output or requirements by good faith and limits disproportionate quantities.

before.note: Every contract imposes on each party a duty of good faith and fair dealing in its performance and its enforcement.

after.note: The Second Restatement states a duty of good faith in performance and enforcement. It is persuasive common-law authority; a jurisdiction must adopt or apply the proposition.

before.note: Where state law does not let parties contract out of the implied covenant, it is a state-imposed duty, so federal airline law preempts it.

after.note: The Airline Deregulation Act preempts this state-imposed covenant claim because it relates to airline prices, routes or services and enlarges voluntarily assumed obligations; ordinary contractual promises remain a separate question.

before.note: Second formulation: drops 'definite and substantial', allows a remedy limited as justice requires, and spares charitable pledges proof of reliance.

after.note: The Second Restatement omits “definite and substantial,” permits a remedy limited as justice requires, and excuses proof of induced reliance for charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements. Adoption varies by jurisdiction.

before.note: Reliance reasoning in public law: a prosecutor's unconditional decision not to charge, made to induce reliance, binds as a matter of due process.

after.note: A separate criminal-law branch: Pennsylvania enforces a prosecutor’s unconditional nonprosecution assurance after detrimental reliance affecting self-incrimination. This is due process, not an ordinary § 90 contract holding.

before.note: Restatement § 45 (1932, kept in 1981): once the offeree begins the invited performance, the offer becomes an option and cannot be revoked.

after.note: For an offer inviting performance rather than a return promise, beginning or tendering the invited performance protects an opportunity to complete it. The offeror’s duty remains conditional on completion; preparation alone is a separate question.

before.fate: Rejected by Drennan (1958); Restatement (Second) § 87(2) follows Drennan

after.fate: Drennan takes a contrary approach in California (1958); § 87(2) later states the reliance approach. Neither overrules this Second Circuit decision.

before.note: A merchant's signed written offer for goods that assures it will be held open is irrevocable without consideration, for no more than three months.

after.note: A merchant’s signed assurance to hold a goods offer open needs no consideration for the stated or reasonable time, capped at three months under § 2-205. An assurance on the offeree’s form must be separately signed.

before.note: Restatement (Second) § 87(2) adopts Drennan: an offer that foreseeably induces substantial reliance before acceptance binds as an option.

after.note: The Second Restatement follows Drennan’s reliance rationale: foreseeable substantial reliance before acceptance can bind an offer as an option to the extent necessary to avoid injustice, not automatically for every use of a bid.

before.note: Between merchants an added term enters the contract unless the objecting party proves it materially alters the deal (New York law).

after.note: Between merchants an additional term enters unless § 2-207(2) excludes it: the offer limits acceptance, the addition materially alters the deal, or timely objection occurs. Bayway assigns the material-alteration burden to the party opposing inclusion.

before.note: Posting amended terms online is not notice to existing users, and a change clause silent about accrued claims does not reach them.

after.note: On this record, website posting and continued use did not give sufficient notice of an arbitration amendment. A separate retroactivity analysis excludes the remaining pre-amendment claims; post-amendment claims had been dismissed by stipulation.

before.fate: Displaced for sales of goods by UCC § 2-209(1) (1952)

after.fate: Section 2-209 supplies a different rule for goods contracts; it does not change this services holding.

before.note: Economic duress makes a coerced price increase voidable: a threat to withhold needed goods with no timely substitute or adequate remedy (New York).

after.note: A separate validity limit: even a modification with consideration is voidable for economic duress when threatened withholding leaves no timely substitute or adequate breach remedy. This does not loosen the pre-existing-duty rule.

before.note: Course of dealing and usage of trade explain or supplement even a final writing, unless they cannot be reconciled with its express terms.

after.note: The 1952 Code’s §§ 1-205 and 2-202 admit dealing and trade usage to explain or supplement a writing. Revised Article 1 later places the combined context rules in § 1-303; irreconcilable express terms prevail.

before.fate: Not followed for home sales in Florida (Johnson v. Davis, 1985) and many other states

after.fate: Johnson adopts a different Florida home-sale rule; it does not overrule this Massachusetts decision.

before.note: Substantial performance: an innocent, trivial deviation is not a failure of condition; the owner gets damages, not forfeiture of the price (New York).

after.note: Substantial performance limits forfeiture for an innocent, trivial construction deviation where the requirement is treated as a promise or constructive condition. It does not generally replace strict compliance with an unmistakable express condition.

before.fate: The Restatement (Third) of Restitution § 38 (2011) caps such recovery at the contract price

after.fate: Restatement (Third) of Restitution § 38 (2011) proposes a contract-price limit. A Restatement does not itself overrule this Fourth Circuit holding.

before.note: Swiss law enforces a penalty without proof of loss but lets the judge reduce an excessive one; a reduction for a minor breach is upheld.

after.note: The assigned translated Swiss decision permits judicial reduction of excessive contractual penalties. This comparative account does not establish the rule in an American jurisdiction.

before.note: The creditor and donee categories give way to one test: intended beneficiaries may enforce the contract, incidental ones may not.

after.note: The Second Restatement replaces its creditor/donee terminology with intended and incidental beneficiaries, conditioned on the contracting parties’ intention. It proposes a framework; it does not enact a uniform state rule.

before.note: No majority on stream of commerce (awareness or something more), but eight Justices find suit unreasonable on fairness grounds alone.

after.note: Eight Justices agree the remaining foreign indemnity suit is unreasonable. No majority chooses between awareness and additional forum-directed conduct as the stream-of-commerce contact test.

before.note: Stream of commerce again without a majority: the plurality demands targeting of the forum; the concurrence holds one sale is not enough.

after.note: Six Justices reject jurisdiction, with no five-Justice rationale: four require state targeting; two concur on the isolated-sale record and decline a broader rule. The three dissenters take a broader market approach.

before.note: Federal statutes stand apart: the Fifth Amendment has no minimum-contacts test, and a narrow statute tied to U.S. conduct is valid.

after.note: A separate federal-statute branch: the Fifth Amendment does not import the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts test. This targeted terrorism statute is valid; the Court leaves the outer limits and a separate reasonableness requirement open.

before.note: A second road: a statute making registration consent to suit on any claim is valid under Pennsylvania Fire, which Shoe did not overrule.

after.note: Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
after.effect: Preserves statutory consent under due process

before.note: Consent by contract: parties may agree in advance to a court's jurisdiction and name an agent to receive process.

after.note: The appointed process agent’s actual prompt forwarding validates service under the Federal Rule despite no advance promise to forward. The Court reserves failed notice and decides no due-process question; it does not approve every boilerplate forum term.
after.effect: Upholds service through an appointed agent

before.note: Consent survives Shoe as presence did in Burnham: registering under a statute that makes registration consent to suit on any claim binds the company.

after.note: Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
after.effect: Preserves statutory consent under due process

before.note: Seizure without a prior hearing is valid when a judge issues the writ on sworn facts, the creditor posts bond and a prompt hearing follows.

after.note: Mitchell sustains Louisiana sequestration for a lien creditor on sworn facts before a judge, with a creditor bond and an immediate debtor hearing. These safeguards qualify Fuentes; not every judge-issued seizure is valid.

before.note: Rule 23 answers whether a class action may proceed and displaces a state bar, but no majority agrees on how to test a Rule's validity.

after.note: Five Justices let the Rule 23 class proceed despite New York’s penalty-class bar. No majority adopts one validity test: Scalia’s plurality reads procedure categorically; Stevens asks whether the state rule defines substantive rights.

before.note: Rule 8 answers what a plaintiff must supply at the outset and really regulates procedure, so it displaces a state affidavit-of-merit law.

after.note: The majority finds Rule 8, reinforced by Rule 12, incompatible with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement. Jackson agrees with the judgment through Rules 3 and 12 while rejecting the majority’s Rule 8 collision analysis.

before.note: A shareholder who verified a complaint in good faith, relying on her adviser's careful investigation, keeps her derivative suit.

after.note: A separate starting point in derivative verification: good-faith reliance on an adviser’s investigation sustains the shareholder’s verification. This is not a holding that subjective good faith defeats modern Rule 11 sanctions.

before.note: Citing cases invented by ChatGPT and standing by them after warnings violates Rule 11(b)(2) and supports sanctions for bad faith.

after.note: The district court applies Rule 11 to invented citations and knowing falsehoods or conscious avoidance after warnings. Its bad-faith requirement addresses court-initiated sanctions in that circuit; the party-motion route has a separate safe harbor.

before.note: The Class Action Fairness Act lets class actions over $5 million in the aggregate proceed on minimal diversity.

after.note: CAFA permits qualifying classes with minimal diversity, an aggregate amount exceeding $5 million and ordinarily at least 100 members, subject to statutory exclusions and exceptions. Ordinary § 1332(a) complete diversity remains.

before.note: The rewritten Rule 23 sets the 23(a) prerequisites and the 23(b) categories, with notice and opt-out for damages classes.

after.note: The 1966 rewrite replaces the true/hybrid/spurious categories with Rule 23(a) and (b), including notice and exclusion rights for (b)(3) damages classes. It reforms procedure rather than merely codifying Hansberry.

before.note: The Federal Arbitration Act preempts state rules that condition arbitration on class procedures, so class waivers stand.

after.note: The FAA preempts California’s rule conditioning arbitration on class procedures. That removes this state-law obstacle to the agreement; it is not a holding that every class waiver is valid under every applicable defense.

after.effect: Rejects an added test in the Ninth Circuit

before.note: After Bristol-Myers, absent class members' claims need no separate showing of specific jurisdiction; the named plaintiff's claims must.

after.note: The Seventh Circuit holds that a federal Rule 23 action under a federal statute needs personal jurisdiction for the named plaintiff, without a separate showing for each absentee. This is a circuit holding, not a Supreme Court resolution of every class setting.
after.effect: Limits Bristol-Myers in the Seventh Circuit

before.note: A movant without the trial burden need not negate the claim; it may point to the absence of evidence, and the opponent must respond.

after.note: After adequate time for discovery, a movant without the trial burden may identify the absence of evidence on an essential element without negating it. Only after that initial showing must the opponent identify a genuine jury issue.

before.note: The 1936 Interpleader Act, now § 1335, opens federal court to a stakeholder whenever two or more adverse claimants are of diverse citizenship.

after.note: Statutory interpleader requires adverse claimants with minimal diversity, a stake worth at least $500, and deposit of the stake or a qualifying bond. The 1936 Act broadens access; these conditions still matter.

before.note: A plurality upholds SORNA's delegation as construed; three dissenters would replace the intelligible-principle test, and Alito would reconsider it.

after.note: Four Justices uphold the delegation after narrowing SORNA by interpretation. Alito supplies the fifth vote under existing doctrine while inviting reconsideration; three dissenters propose a stricter approach. No majority replaces the intelligible-principle test.

before.note: Seila reaches the FHFA's single Director too, but an invalid removal shield voids nothing unless it actually caused the harm.

after.note: Seila’s single-director rule reaches the FHFA. Because the officer was properly appointed, the unconstitutional removal restriction does not automatically invalidate past actions; retrospective relief requires compensable harm caused by the restriction.

before.note: The same day the Federal Reserve is set apart: its structure stands, and removing a governor for cause requires notice and a chance to respond.

after.note: The Court denies a stay of Cook’s preliminary protection: removal is reviewable and the statute requires notice and an opportunity to respond. It treats the Federal Reserve’s history separately and leaves the precise definition of cause open.
after.effect: Preserves the Fed separately at the stay stage
Rejects seizure; Jackson supplies a framework
Splits over statutory control of process

before.note: SEC civil penalties for securities fraud are legal claims that need a jury in an Article III court; the public-rights exception does not reach them.

after.note: SEC fraud penalties resemble a common-law legal claim and require an Article III jury. The Court distinguishes Atlas Roofing rather than overruling it; public rights and other kinds of agency adjudication remain separate questions.

before.note: When the agency's reasoning contains a legal error, the court must remand under Chenery, not affirm on its own corrected analysis.

after.note: A legal error in an agency’s discretionary reasoning ordinarily requires Chenery remand; the court may not simply substitute its own corrected analysis. Narrow remand exceptions are not a general license to supply agency policy.

after.effect: Finds a likely defect at the stay stage
Specific order upheld; rule rationale divided

before.note: A general grant of power to make rules lets the FTC issue binding substantive rules, a real alternative to case-by-case enforcement.

after.note: The D.C. Circuit reads the FTC Act’s general rulemaking clause to authorize binding rules defining unfair or deceptive practices. The holding concerns that statutory scheme, not every agency’s general rulemaking clause.

before.note: For adjudication, a statutory 'public hearing' on disputed facts can trigger formal APA procedure without the words 'on the record'.

after.note: A separate adjudication branch: the Ninth Circuit reads a statutory “public hearing” on disputed facts to trigger formal APA adjudication without “on the record.” This does not expand formal rulemaking under Florida East Coast.

after.effect: Finds likely notice failure on this proposal

before.note: A rule is legislative if it supplies the basis for enforcement, appears in the CFR, invokes legislative authority or amends a legislative rule.

after.note: The D.C. Circuit lists indicia of legislative rules: an independent enforcement basis, CFR publication, express legislative authority or amendment of a legislative rule. Later cases focus on legal effect; publication alone is not a universal conclusive test.

before.note: Concrete injury needs a close historical analogue; every class member seeking damages must have it, and unrealized risk is not enough.

after.note: Every member recovering damages needs concrete injury. For intangible injury the Court asks for a close historical analogue; an unmaterialized risk alone does not support retrospective damages, though prospective relief is a separate inquiry.
